walkthroughs.body_html:
How the Market Works — a core area of GCSE Economics.

Working through it builds the schema you need: the key terms, how they connect, and how to use them together.

How the Market Works brings together several ideas you need to use as a set, not in isolation.

Lock in the vocabulary first, then practise pulling the ideas together to answer real questions.

Use the activities in this adventure to build familiarity with How the Market Works.

Practise vocabulary, calculations and free-text questions to lock in the learning.

mcqs.q: The demand for labour is described as derived because it depends on:
options: Wage rates
Demand for output
Union power
Tax rates

mcqs.q: The UK Equality Act was passed in:
What is the difference between a shift in demand and a movement along the demand curve?
options: A change in price shifts the demand curve.
Comparative advantage means richer countries should help poorer ones.
A movement along the curve is caused by a change in price; a shift of the whole curve is caused by changes in other factors (income, tastes, substitute prices).
Demand always falls when supply increases.

mcqs.q: What is the difference between revenue and profit?
options: Revenue is profit before tax and profit is revenue after tax.
Revenue is total income from sales (price x quantity); profit is what remains after deducting costs from revenue.
Revenue and profit mean the same thing.
Comparative advantage means richer countries should help poorer ones.

mcqs.q: What is the principle of comparative advantage?
options: Countries should specialise in producing goods with lower opportunity cost relative to others — even a country worse at everything still has a comparative advantage in something.
Revenue is profit before tax and profit is revenue after tax.
Comparative advantage means richer countries should help poorer ones.
A country should produce whatever it can make best.
